In the experimental setup, RF being situated between both conduction-enabled chambers, the application of the field was to ensure significant boosting of the pocket-based drying coupled with the increase in sample energy due to the contact cycles. Figure 10 depicts the instantaneous moisture content as a function of drying time for a 300 GSM 800 W RF+Base trial. A closer look at the figure shows intermittent drops in the moisture content, similar to the behavior seen in RF+convection, indicating the effect of RF in the drying process and the improvements seen. The sample temperature and drying rate (as shown in Figure 12) as a function of moisture content also depict the influence of RF on these parameters and indicate the increase in heating of the sample, thereby increasing the rate of water removal as well. Here again, the increase in sample temperature matches closely with increases in drying rate at a given moisture content. An interesting behavior seen in both sample temperature and drying rate plots is that under an X = 0.4 moisture content, the RF being less effective in the RF+Base trials, as seen in the RF+Convection only trials, indicating the high dependency of moisture content for the electric field to produce effective results. It is clearly seen that after the first three pulses of RF, the increase in drying rates is not visible at all, inferring that RF applied in lower moisture levels is not being absorbed by the sample and, hence, the applied RF energy is not being utilized. At higher sheet moisture contents, there is higher drying rate and water removal corresponding with higher absorption of energy. As the moisture content nears the end of the drying cycle, the effect of RF is minimal, and this leads to a decrease in drying rate in comparison to the pre-RF drying regime. This clearly shows the efficacy of RF application at higher moisture contents.
